**PR(A) = (1 − d) + d (PR(T1)/C(T1) + … + PR(Tn)/C(Tn))**

- **T1…Tn** are the pages that point to page A, which the paper calls "citations." (p. 109)
- **d** is a damping factor that can be set between 0 and 1. The authors usually set it to 0.85. (p. 109)
- **C(T)** is the number of links going out of page T. So each linking page's PageRank is divided by its number of outgoing links. (p. 110)

**Why it's built this way:** PageRank extends simple citation counting in two ways. It does not count links from all pages equally, and it normalizes by the number of links on a page. (p. 109)

**Other properties the paper states:**
- The PageRanks form a probability distribution over Web pages, so all pages' PageRanks sum to one. (p. 110)
- PR(A) can be computed with a simple iterative algorithm. It corresponds to the principal eigenvector of the normalized link matrix of the Web. (p. 110)
- PageRank for 26 million pages can be computed in a few hours on a medium-size workstation. (p. 110)

**Intuitive interpretation:** A "random surfer" starts on a random page and keeps clicking links, never hitting "back." Eventually the surfer gets bored and jumps to another random page. PageRank is the probability that the surfer visits a page. The paper describes d as the probability that, at each page, the surfer gets bored and requests another random page. (p. 110)

A page can therefore have a high PageRank in two ways. Many pages can point to it, or a few pages with high PageRank can point to it. (p. 110)
